text.p: Joining a health club can cost hundreds of dollars, so for most people it's no casual decision. The trick is to ensure your money is well spent and does not disappear down the (steamroom) drain.
Clubs range from bare-bones exercise centres to fully appointed, opulent spas. But before signing up at one advertised by a bikini-clad beach babe or muscle-bound power lifter, do some research.
More than 11 percent of Americans over age 18 exercise in a health club. But at $600 to $1,000 a year for many private clubs, it's a big chunk of most people's pay.
Whether your goal is to look like someone from "Baywatch," train for a triathlon or just work off stress, choosing the club that's right for you is crucial.
"The first thing is sit down and ask yourself what your goals are," said Kyle Merker, who writes about fitness from New York.
Do you want to lose weight, tone, swim, play basketball, meet someone? All these goals are legitimate but some clubs may be more appropriate than others.
Decide where you want to be. Do you want a gym near home, near work or your child's day care center?
Next, Merker said, list your needs and wants. You need a treadmill, for example, a pool, or a basketball court. You want a place that provides towels and hairdriers.
Then consider what you can afford.
With these various lists in hand, "start to see what's out there and what's reasonable. Compare prices," he said.

Beware that quoted club fees may contain hidden costs. For example, a club might have monthly dues or an initiation fee. It may charge extra for lockers or towels, personal training or classes, or use of tennis or squash courts. If fees are not spelled out in full, ask.
"Don't feel pressured to sign up today. There is always a 'sale' going on because if one 'sale' ends today, another starts tomorrow," Merker said.

Ask for a lower price than the one quoted. Often, if you mention that X Club charges a certain amount, Y Club may try to match it. If that's not possible, ask for an extra month, some free services, a T-shirt -- anything.

Merker also recommended that when joining a club, ask if club management will guarantee the renewal price for life -- your life, not the life of the club, since you're likely to "stay in business" longer than many a health club.

Also, spend time at the club before you pay to join. Ask a senior manager if you can have a free tryout day, or if that's not possible, pay the day fee and check it out. Go when you would normally use the club, test the equipment, check out the crowd. It's a chance to ask members about the facilities.
Then, if you decide to join, ask if the club will credit you whatever you spent on the day fee. For your membership, many clubs will say yes.
Cleanliness is one criterion that should never be ignored.
"It's perfectly OK to ask about the cleaning schedule," Merker said. Also ask whether the club requires people to wear footwear in showers, swimcaps in the pool and so on.
You've checked out what you can see, now check out what you can't see -- the club's background.

It's wise to call the health club's main office, if your local one is a franchise, to check the club's status. You also can check advertisements in body building magazines, where many chains advertise, to see if your local gym or club is among those listed. Some health clubs hope to capitalise on popular gym names, but actually are in no way related.
Also, call the Better Business Bureau or department of consumer affairs to ask if any complaints have been lodged against the club.
"A smart consumer does his homework upfront, and that is your best protection," Merker said. Recouping lost money is difficult and not always successful if a club goes out of business.
If your club is part of a chain or a YM- or YWCA, you may be able to use facilities in other cities or other parts of town. Some have reciprocal memberships.
Merker said YM/YWCAs were a "great deal. With Ys, yo know what you get. I've never been disappointed at a Y."
Merker's new book, "The Fitness Guide: Where to work out when you're on the road," (Incline Press) can be ordered for $14.95 by calling 1 800 833-1543.
